opts: To ensure that every bank remains highly profitable.
Because they are guardians of people's wealth.
To reduce the level of competition among banks.
To increase the total number of banks in the system.
questionBank.exp: Banks are guardians of people's wealth and must be checked for the benefit of depositors and stakeholders (p.26).

questionBank.q: Bank examination looks at all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: How well risks are managed.
The bank's marketing strategies.
How much risk the bank undertakes.
What resources are available to support business and risk profile.
questionBank.exp: Examination looks at risk, management, and resources, not marketing strategies (p.26).

questionBank.q: The impact of bank supervision on the financial system includes:
opts: Market transparency and discipline.
All of the above.
Financial stability and safety.
Deposit insurance and protection.
questionBank.exp: Supervision contributes to stability, transparency, deposit protection, and compliance (p.26-27).

questionBank.q: Routine on-site examination of banks is presently conducted how often?
opts: Once a year.
Twice a year.
Three times a year.
Quarterly.
questionBank.exp: Routine on-site examination is conducted twice a year (p.27).

questionBank.q: The two types of routine on-site examinations mentioned are:
opts: Liquidity assessment and capital assessment.
Risk Assets assessment and Risk Based Supervision.
Financial audit and compliance audit.
Forensic audit and fraud investigation.
questionBank.exp: Routine examinations are Risk Assets assessment and Risk Based Supervision (p.27).

questionBank.q: Nigeria has adopted which approach to banking supervision in line with international best practice?
opts: Rules-based supervision.
Risk-based supervision.
Principle-based supervision.
Proactive supervision.
questionBank.exp: Nigeria has opted for a Risk-based Supervision (RBS) approach (p.27).

questionBank.q: Risk Based Supervision (RBS) involves:
opts: Applying the CAMELS framework to score management quality.
Identifying significant activities and determining inherent risks.
Classifying non-performing loans into sub-standard, doubtful, and lost categories.
Conducting a special investigation triggered by a depositor petition.
questionBank.exp: RBS involves identification of activities, determination of risks, evaluation of risk management, and determination of overall riskiness (p.27).

questionBank.q: Macro-prudential supervision aims to:
opts: Focusing narrowly on the safety of one individual bank at a time.
Complement micro-prudential supervision by considering threats to the whole financial system.
Replace the CAMELS framework used in routine bank examination.
Replace micro-prudential supervision of individual banks altogether.
questionBank.exp: Macro-prudential supervision complements traditional supervision of individual banks with consideration of systemic threats (p.27).

questionBank.q: The ultimate goal of macro-prudential supervision is to:
opts: Increasing the profitability of individual banks.
Minimise systemic risk that could damage the broader economy.
Increasing the fees regulators charge for supervision.
Reducing the total number of licensed banks.
questionBank.exp: Goal is to minimise systemic risk that could inflict significant damage on the broader economy (p.27).

questionBank.q: Which type of examination is conducted as at the financial year end of every bank (31st December)?
opts: Foreign Exchange Examination.
Routine Risk Assessment Examination.
Special examination.
Special Investigation.
questionBank.exp: Routine Risk Assessment Examination is conducted as at the financial year end (p.28).

questionBank.q: The Routine Risk Assessment Examination primarily reviews:
opts: The bank's corporate governance structures and fit-and-proper status of directors.
All assets on the balance sheet to check for impairments.
Petitions received from the banking public about specific transactions.
Compliance with foreign exchange rules and sources and application of funds.
questionBank.exp: It reviews all assets on the balance sheet for impairments (p.28).

questionBank.q: A special examination is conducted when:
opts: The bank itself requesting a special examination.
The regulatory authorities have cause to believe safety and soundness have been impaired.
The bank simply opening a new branch office.
The bank's CAR falling below the 10% prudential minimum during a routine review.
questionBank.exp: Special examination is conducted when safety and soundness are considerably impaired (p.28).

questionBank.q: A special examination is a statutory examination and is:
opts: Limited to reviewing a bank's compliance with KYC procedures.
A prelude to regulatory intervention.
A routine annual check.
Conducted twice yearly as part of routine risk assessment.
questionBank.exp: It is a prelude to regulatory intervention (p.28).

questionBank.q: Foreign Exchange Examination is conducted to check compliance with:
opts: Anti-money laundering rules.
Forex rules and regulations.
Corporate governance rules.
Capital adequacy requirements.
questionBank.exp: It checks compliance with forex rules and regulations (p.28).

questionBank.q: Special investigations are unscheduled examinations arising from:
opts: A routine annual examination plan drawn up in advance.
Petitions from the banking public or suspicions.
An injection of fresh capital into the bank.
Changes in management.
questionBank.exp: Special investigations arise from petitions, suspicions, or prior examination activities (p.28).

questionBank.q: At the end of every examination, a report of findings is produced. The report must be:
opts: Published in full to the general public without restriction.
Factual and supported by credible documentary evidence.
Withheld from discussion with the bank's own management team.
Based on assumptions.
questionBank.exp: Reports must be factual and assertions supported with evidence (p.28-29).

questionBank.q: Examination findings must be discussed with management, and management explanations must be factored into the final report. This is described as:
opts: A privileged system.
An open reporting system.
A confidential system.
A closed reporting system.
questionBank.exp: It is an open reporting system with no surprises (p.29).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a type of bank examination?
opts: Routine Risk Assessment.
Financial Audit.
Foreign Exchange Examination.
Special Examination.
questionBank.exp: Types: Routine Risk Assessment, Special, Foreign Exchange, and Special Investigations. Financial Audit is not listed (p.28).

questionBank.q: The CBN and NDIC carry out examinations to determine:
opts: The marketing strategies employed by individual banks.
Solvency status and compliance with laws.
The preferences and satisfaction levels of bank customers.
The satisfaction levels of the bank's own employees.
questionBank.exp: Examinations determine solvency and compliance (p.25).

questionBank.q: Early Warning Signals (EWS) are used to:
opts: Reducing the level of regulatory oversight over banks.
Detect ill-health and take prompt corrective action.
Increasing the profitability of individual banks.
Encouraging new entrants into the banking sector.
questionBank.exp: EWS detects ill-health and leads to Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) (p.26).

questionBank.q: Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) refers to:
opts: Simply reducing the interest rates a troubled bank charges.
Taking appropriate action to restore a troubled bank to good standing.
Extending fresh loans directly to a troubled bank.
Ordering the immediate liquidation of any troubled bank.
questionBank.exp: PCA is taking appropriate corrective action to restore a troubled bank (p.26).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is an objective of bank supervision?
opts: To increase the market share held by individual banks.
To ensure compliance with regulations and laws.
To maximise the profits earned by bank shareholders.
To reduce the level of customer service banks provide.
questionBank.exp: Supervision ensures compliance and protection (p.26-27).

questionBank.q: Bank supervision helps to promote:
opts: Unfair practices.
Operational resilience.
High staff turnover.
High loan default rates.
questionBank.exp: Supervision promotes operational resilience, among other benefits (p.27).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a component of the supervisory structure?
opts: Licensing requirements.
All of the above.
Capital adequacy rules.
Safety net arrangements.
questionBank.exp: Supervisory structure includes licensing, capital, accounting, disclosure, risk management (p.10).

questionBank.q: The Basel Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision include the principle that supervisors should have:
opts: The power to hire and dismiss individual bank staff.
Power to revoke licences and take corrective actions.
The power to directly manage a bank's day-to-day operations.
The power to set the interest rates banks may charge.
questionBank.exp: Core Principles include supervisory powers like revocation and corrective actions (p.10).

questionBank.q: Nigeria's compliance with the 29 Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision is described as:
opts: Non-compliant.
Largely compliant.
Fully compliant.
Partially compliant.
questionBank.exp: Nigeria is largely compliant with the Core Principles (p.27).

questionBank.q: Risk-based supervision focuses on:
opts: Compliance with cash reserve requirements.
The overall riskiness of the bank's business.
The classification of loans as sub-standard, doubtful, or lost.
Whether the bank has been designated a systemically important bank.
questionBank.exp: RBS determines the overall riskiness of the bank's business (p.27).

questionBank.q: The macro-prudential approach is concerned with:
opts: The safety and soundness of a single bank in isolation.
The stability of the financial system as a whole.
The profitability recorded by individual banks.
The operational efficiency of payment systems alone.
questionBank.exp: Macro-prudential approach focuses on systemic stability (p.27).

questionBank.q: Special investigations are typically triggered by:
opts: A routine annual review scheduled well in advance.
Petitions from the banking public.
A routine change in a bank's senior management.
An increase in the bank's paid-up capital.
questionBank.exp: They arise from petitions, suspicions, or prior examinations (p.28).

questionBank.q: The report of examination findings is described as an open reporting system because:
opts: Findings are published directly in national newspapers.
Findings are discussed with management and their responses included.
Findings are made freely available to the general public.
Findings are shared with every other bank in the industry.
questionBank.exp: It is open because findings are discussed with management and responses factored in (p.29).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a benefit of off-site supervision?
opts: It provides real-time insight into bank operations.
It is less costly than on-site.
It reduces the need for statutory returns.
It allows physical verification of assets.
questionBank.exp: Off-site is less costly, though it relies on returns (p.26).

questionBank.q: Regulatory authorities in emerging markets often rely more on off-site supervision because:
opts: They lack trained staff.
They have limited resources.
They prefer remote work.
They have no regulatory powers.
questionBank.exp: Emerging markets with inadequate resources rely more on off-site supervision (p.26).

questionBank.q: Bank supervision is critical to mitigate:
opts: Exchange rates.
Banking crises.
Interest rates.
Bank profits.
questionBank.exp: Banking crisis is best mitigated through effective supervision (p.26).

questionBank.q: The Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria (AMCON) was established to:
opts: Provide deposit insurance to customers of licensed banks.
Purchase toxic risk assets of ailing banks.
Regulate stock exchanges and other capital market operators.
Formulate and implement the CBN's monetary policy.
questionBank.exp: AMCON was set up to purchase toxic assets to improve liquidity (p.32).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a duty of bank supervisors under the curative role?
opts: Prescribe capital requirements.
Take over management of ailing banks.
Conduct fit and proper tests.
Issue banking licences.
questionBank.exp: Curative role includes injecting funds and taking over management (p.32).

questionBank.q: The preventive role of bank supervisors includes:
opts: Purchasing the toxic risk assets of already-ailing banks.
Entry point screening of shareholders and managers.
Taking over the management of a distressed bank.
Winding up the affairs of a bank whose licence has been revoked.
questionBank.exp: Preventive role includes entry point screening (fit and proper) and capital prescription (p.31).

questionBank.q: The curative role of bank supervisors includes all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Taking over management.
Issuing banking licences.
Setting up AMCON.
Injecting funds into troubled banks.
questionBank.exp: Issuing licences is preventive, not curative (p.31-32).

questionBank.q: The liquidation role of bank supervisors aims to:
opts: Preventing bank failures before they occur.
Ensure smooth winding up and maximise asset realisation for depositors.
Reducing the overall regulatory burden on banks.
Maximising the returns received by the bank's shareholders.
questionBank.exp: Liquidation role aims for orderly winding up and best possible revenue for depositors (p.32).

questionBank.q: A bank that is critically undercapitalised (CAR <2%) is subject to:
opts: Restriction on dividends.
Takeover of management and/or revocation of licence.
Request for a business plan showing how fresh capital will be raised.
Special examination.
questionBank.exp: Critically undercapitalised may lead to takeover/revocation (p.23).

questionBank.q: The CBN's power to impose sanctions on banks includes:
opts: Removal of directors.
All of the above.
Suspension from forex transactions.
Monetary penalty.
questionBank.exp: Sanctions include fines, removal, suspension, takeover, and revocation (p.31).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a consequence of non-compliance with banking regulations?
opts: Increased profitability.
Fines and suspension from clearing.
More favourable interest rates.
Reduced regulatory oversight.
questionBank.exp: Non-compliance leads to penalties, suspension, removal, etc. (p.32).

questionBank.q: The CBN's intervention in a failing bank may include:
opts: Approving new loan applications on the bank's behalf.
Injecting funds and taking over management.
Reducing the minimum capital requirements applicable to the bank.
Waiving all penalties previously imposed on the bank.
questionBank.exp: Intervention includes injecting funds and taking over management (p.32).

questionBank.q: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) shares supervision of deposit money banks with:
opts: The SEC.
The CBN.
The EFCC.
The FMF.
questionBank.exp: NDIC shares supervision with CBN (p.4).

questionBank.q: On-site examination includes:
opts: Desk review of bank data.
Physically authenticating periodic reports.
Analyzing financial statements sent to CBN.
Reviewing statutory returns.
questionBank.exp: On-site consists of physically authenticating reports (p.25).

questionBank.q: Off-site supervision relies on:
opts: Interviews conducted directly with the bank's customers.
Mandatory statutory returns periodically sent to CBN.
Review of the bank's own internal audit reports.
Physical inspection of the bank's branch premises.
questionBank.exp: Off-site comprises receipt and analysis of mandatory statutory returns (p.26).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a key element of Risk-Based Supervision?
opts: Counting cash in vaults.
Evaluating the risk management framework.
Reviewing all loan applications.
Checking all transactions for compliance.
questionBank.exp: RBS involves evaluating risk management framework (p.27).

questionBank.q: The macro-prudential approach supports micro-prudential supervision but cannot:
opts: Enhance it.
Replace it.
Improve it.
Complement it.
questionBank.exp: Macro-prudential supervision can only support, not supplant, micro-prudential supervision (p.27).

questionBank.q: A special examination is ordered when:
opts: The bank declares a dividend.
There is a threat to safety and soundness.
The bank's CAR falls below 10%.
The bank opens a new branch.
questionBank.exp: Special examination is when safety and soundness are considerably impaired (p.28).

questionBank.q: Foreign Exchange Examination reviews:
opts: The bank's capital adequacy ratio as at year end.
Sources and application of funds and forex compliance.
The competence of the bank's management team.
The quality of the assets held on the bank's balance sheet.
questionBank.exp: It reviews sources and application of funds (p.28).

questionBank.q: Special investigations are:
opts: Scheduled annually.
Unscheduled and arise from petitions.
Conducted at the bank's financial year end as part of asset quality review.
Triggered whenever a bank's CAR falls below 10%, as a scheduled review.
questionBank.exp: They are unscheduled from petitions or suspicions (p.28).

questionBank.q: The report of examination findings must be:
opts: Published immediately in the national press.
Supported with credible documentary evidence.
Based on hearsay gathered during the examination.
Kept confidential and withheld from the bank.
questionBank.exp: Assertions must be supported with evidence (p.28-29).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a role of bank supervisors?
opts: Curative.
Promotional.
Liquidative.
Preventive.
questionBank.exp: The three roles are preventive, curative, and liquidation (p.30-32).

questionBank.q: The preventive role includes ensuring that individuals with questionable integrity are precluded from owning or managing banks through:
opts: Educational qualifications.
Fit and proper person test.
Police clearance.
Political affiliation.
questionBank.exp: Fit and proper person test is used to prevent undesirable persons from entering banking (p.31).

questionBank.q: Capital adequacy as a preventive measure aims to:
opts: Reducing the total number of banks operating in the system.
Ensure banks have enough capital to support their operations and absorb losses.
Encouraging banks to take on riskier lending than their capital can support.
Increasing the profitability of individual banks.
questionBank.exp: Capital adequacy provides cushion against losses and supports operations (p.31).

questionBank.q: Continuous supervision includes:
opts: Foreign exchange examinations conducted to check compliance with forex rules.
On-site and off-site supervision diligently executed.
Special investigations arising from suspicions of malpractice.
Special examinations ordered whenever a depositor files a petition.
questionBank.exp: Continuous supervision involves both on-site and off-site (p.31).

questionBank.q: Information disclosure as a preventive tool requires banks to announce:
opts: The private financial details of individual customers.
Operating results to the public.
The bank's confidential internal strategic plans.
The findings contained in internal audit reports.
questionBank.exp: Banks must disclose operating results to inform stakeholders (p.31).

questionBank.q: Imposition of sanctions is a preventive measure. Which of the following is a sanction?
opts: Removal of directors.
All of the above.
Suspension from clearing house.
Payment of monetary penalty.
questionBank.exp: Sanctions include fines, removal, suspension, takeover, revocation (p.31).

questionBank.q: The curative role aims to correct anomalies and prevent:
opts: An increase in the profits earned by the affected bank.
Loss of confidence or run on banks.
The entry of new banks into the market.
A reduction in the bank's regulatory capital.
questionBank.exp: Curative role corrects anomalies to prevent loss of confidence (p.32).

questionBank.q: AMCON was set up to purchase toxic assets from ailing banks. This is part of the:
opts: Liquidation role.
Curative role.
Supervisory role.
Preventive role.
questionBank.exp: AMCON is a curative measure to improve bank liquidity (p.32).

questionBank.q: Liquidation role ensures that depositors do not face avoidable loss through:
opts: Reducing the level of deposit insurance coverage available.
Orderly winding up and asset realisation.
Relying on government bailouts to cover depositor losses.
Waiving the liabilities owed to the bank's creditors.
questionBank.exp: Liquidation ensures smooth winding up and best possible revenue (p.32).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a consequence of non-compliance with banking laws?
opts: A reduction in the penalties imposed for non-compliance.
Revocation of banking licence.
Higher capital adequacy for the offending bank.
Increased public trust in the offending bank.
questionBank.exp: Non-compliance may lead to licence revocation (p.32).

questionBank.q: Effective collaboration by regulatory authorities is required for:
opts: Lower capital requirements imposed on banks.
Good corporate governance and safe banking.
Increased profitability for individual banks.
A general reduction in banking regulation.
questionBank.exp: Collaboration ensures good governance and safe banking (p.32).

questionBank.q: Risk management practices such as the COSO Framework and Basel Accords are adopted to maintain:
opts: Maintaining a low level of competition among banks.
International best practice.
Keeping interest rates high across the banking sector.
Maximising the profits earned by individual banks.
questionBank.exp: Adoption maintains international best practice and sustainable risk management (p.4).

questionBank.q: The CBN's adoption of the Basel Accords requires banks to maintain:
opts: High loan-to-deposit ratios across the banking sector.
Certain levels of capital and liquidity.
Low operational costs relative to income.
High dividend payouts to shareholders.
questionBank.exp: Basel Accords require capital and liquidity to reduce systemic risk (p.25).

questionBank.q: Under the preventive role, prescription of capital is important because:
opts: Capital adequacy is reviewed once every three years, alongside the credit policy.
Higher capital reduces likelihood of failure.
Capital is not important for banks.
Lower capital increases returns.
questionBank.exp: Higher capital makes a bank less likely to fail (p.31).

questionBank.q: The liquidation role is necessary when:
opts: A bank continuing to operate profitably.
A bank fails and its licence is revoked.
A bank simply opening a new branch office.
A bank declaring dividends to its shareholders.
questionBank.exp: Liquidation is for failed banks whose licences are revoked (p.32).

questionBank.q: The CBN's power to take over management of a bank is an example of:
opts: Preventive role.
Curative role.
Liquidation role.
Regulatory role.
questionBank.exp: Takeover of management is curative (p.32).

questionBank.q: Off-site supervision is less effective in emerging markets because of:
opts: Strong banking culture.
Inadequate resources.
High competition.
High level of technology.
questionBank.exp: Emerging markets with inadequate resources rely more on off-site (p.26).

questionBank.q: The Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision are issued by:
opts: The International Monetary Fund, as part of its surveillance role.
The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision.
The World Bank, as part of its development mandate.
The United Nations, as part of its economic agencies.
questionBank.exp: The Basel Committee issues the Core Principles (p.10).

questionBank.q: Special investigations are conducted to ascertain the true position of issues under investigation. They are triggered by:
opts: Routine changes in a bank's senior management.
Petitions from the banking public.
Routine annual checks scheduled in advance.
An injection of fresh capital into the bank.
questionBank.exp: They arise from petitions, suspicions, or prior examinations (p.28).

questionBank.q: The report of examination findings must be discussed with management to:
opts: Avoid confrontation.
Ensure an open reporting system.
Keep findings secret.
Delay regulatory action.
questionBank.exp: Discussion with management and inclusion of responses is an open system (p.29).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a benefit of effective bank supervision?
opts: Higher profits earned by individual banks.
Enhanced market transparency and discipline.
A reduction in the level of regulatory oversight.
Lower capital requirements imposed on banks.
questionBank.exp: Supervision enhances transparency and discipline (p.26-27).

questionBank.q: The macro-prudential approach aims to minimise systemic risk by considering:
opts: Sensitivity to interest rate and exchange rate movements for a single bank.
Interconnections among financial institutions.
Classification of non-performing loans within one institution.
The capital adequacy ratio of a single bank in isolation.
questionBank.exp: Macro-prudential considers threats to the financial system as a whole (p.27).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a tool used in off-site supervision?
opts: Physical visits to the bank's branch premises.
Analysis of statutory returns.
Interviews conducted directly with the bank's customers.
A physical count of the bank's cash holdings.
questionBank.exp: Off-site relies on analysis of statutory returns (p.26).

questionBank.q: On-site supervision provides the advantage of:
opts: The lower cost of conducting the examination.
Physical authentication of reports.
A reduced overall regulatory burden on the bank.
A faster turnaround in analysing the bank's returns.
questionBank.exp: On-site allows physical authentication (p.25).

questionBank.q: The CBN and NDIC carry out routine examinations twice a year. This is to:
opts: Increasing the profitability of the examined banks.
Ensure ongoing safety and soundness.
Reducing the cost of conducting the examination.
Meeting requirements imposed by the Basel Committee.
questionBank.exp: Routine examinations ensure safety and soundness (p.27).

questionBank.q: Risk-based supervision shifts focus from:
opts: Capital adequacy assessment to liquidity assessment.
Transaction-based checking to risk management assessment.
Compliance checking to product innovation.
Profitability analysis to market share analysis.
questionBank.exp: RBS focuses on risk management rather than just transactions (p.27).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a component of the supervisory review process under Pillar II of Basel II?
opts: Minimum capital requirements prescribed under Pillar I.
Supervisory review and risk management.
Liquidity requirements prescribed to manage funding risk.
Market discipline achieved through public disclosure.
questionBank.exp: Pillar II is supervisory review (p.8).

questionBank.q: The Nigerian banking sector's supervision is largely compliant with the 29 Core Principles, which include:
opts: Banks in emerging markets should abandon on-site examination in favour of off-site review.
Supervisors must have the authority to take corrective actions.
Banks must have unlimited deposit insurance.
Banks must be state-owned.
questionBank.exp: Core Principles include supervisory powers for corrective actions (p.10).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a type of risk that the macro-prudential approach addresses?
opts: Credit risk.
Systemic risk.
Liquidity risk.
Operational risk.
questionBank.exp: Macro-prudential addresses systemic risk (p.27).

questionBank.q: The CBN's circular on false returns is designed to:
opts: Encourage bank mergers.
Ensure data integrity.
Increase bank profits.
Reduce regulatory oversight.
questionBank.exp: It ensures data integrity (p.23).

questionBank.q: A bank that fails to report a serial dud cheque issuer may be penalised under:
opts: EFCC Act.
BOFIA.
NDIC Act.
CBN Act.
questionBank.exp: Failure is concealment and misrepresentation, punished under BOFIA (p.24-25).

questionBank.q: The Prudential Guidelines require that banks obtain credit reports from at least two credit bureaux. This is to:
opts: Increase costs.
Enhance credit risk assessment.
Reduce lending.
Comply with the single obligor limit calculation.
questionBank.exp: It enhances assessment of borrowers (p.20).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a criterion for a facility to be classified as 'lost'?
opts: Interest unpaid for 90 days.
Principal unpaid for 360 days or more.
Facility is fully secured.
Borrower has good cash flow.
questionBank.exp: Lost: 360 days or more (p.22).

questionBank.q: The haircut adjustment on collateral for provisioning requires that collateral be:
opts: Based on book value.
Perfected and realisable.
Valued using the historic cost method without adjustment.
Unperfected but acceptable.
questionBank.exp: Must be perfected and realisable (p.22).

questionBank.q: Revaluation of fixed assets requires CBN approval and is allowed only for:
opts: Investment properties.
Own premises.
Intangible assets.
Equipment.
questionBank.exp: Only own premises (p.22).

questionBank.q: The discount on revaluation surplus is 55%, meaning:
opts: 55% is written off.
Only 45% of the surplus can be recognised.
45% is discounted.
55% of the surplus is added to capital.
questionBank.exp: Discount of 55% means 45% of the surplus is recognised (p.22).

questionBank.q: A bank's CAR of 6% would trigger which supervisory action?
opts: Revoke licence.
Restrict dividend distribution.
Take over management.
Restrict new lending to recoveries.
questionBank.exp: Under capitalised (5-10%) → restrict dividends (p.23).

questionBank.q: A bank with CAR of 3% is significantly undercapitalised. What action may CBN take?
opts: Immediately classifying all of the bank's loans as lost.
Request a business plan for capital injection.
Immediately revoking the bank's operating licence.
Taking no supervisory action at all.
questionBank.exp: Significantly undercapitalised: request business plan, restrict lending (p.23).

questionBank.q: The Banking Sector Resolution Fund is used for:
opts: Funding regulatory agencies.
Paying operating costs of a bridge bank.
Providing loans to customers.
Paying dividends to shareholders.
questionBank.exp: Fund used for bridge bank costs, transfer costs, credit facilities (p.18).

questionBank.q: The CBN may freeze an account under Section 97 of BOFIA if the Governor believes:
opts: The account has insufficient funds.
Transactions involve a criminal offence.
The account is dormant.
The customer is a director.
questionBank.exp: Freeze if transactions involve criminal offence (p.18).

questionBank.q: The Special Tribunal for the Enforcement and Recovery of Eligible Loans is established under:
opts: Section 53 of BOFIA.
Section 102 of BOFIA.
Section 74 of BOFIA.
Section 12 of BOFIA.
questionBank.exp: Section 102 establishes the Tribunal (p.19).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a consequence of non-compliance with banking laws?
opts: Increase in capital.
Blacklisting of officers.
Higher dividends.
Reduction in interest rates.
questionBank.exp: Non-compliance may lead to blacklisting of officers (p.32).

questionBank.q: The CBN's power to impose sanctions is derived from:
opts: The National Assembly.
Its enabling statutes.
The Federal Ministry of Finance.
The Constitution.
questionBank.exp: Regulators are empowered by enabling statutes to impose sanctions (p.31).

questionBank.q: Bank supervisors enforce adequate disclosure to ensure that:
opts: Discouraging healthy competition among licensed banks.
Governments, supervisors, depositors, and investors are informed of bank performance.
Helping banks maximise their reported quarterly profits.
Encouraging banks to reduce their overall lending activity.
questionBank.exp: Disclosure informs all stakeholders (p.31).

questionBank.q: The CAMELS parameters are used by the CBN to evaluate:
opts: The customer satisfaction of banks.
The well-being of banks.
The market share of banks.
The profitability of banks.
questionBank.exp: CAMELS is used to evaluate well-being of banks (p.29).

questionBank.q: The 'C' in CAMELS stands for:
opts: Credit Quality.
Capital Adequacy.
Customer Satisfaction.
Compliance.
questionBank.exp: C stands for Capital Adequacy (p.29).

questionBank.q: What constitutes the core capital of a bank?
opts: Deposits placed with the bank by its customers.
Equity contributions, reserves, and retained earnings.
Grants received by the bank from the Federal Government.
Funds borrowed by the bank from other banks.
questionBank.exp: Core capital includes equity, reserves, and retained earnings (p.29).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a function of bank capital?
opts: Reducing the bank's day-to-day operating costs.
Provides support for the volume and character of the bank's business.
Funding the payment of dividends to shareholders.
Financing the deposits placed with the bank by customers.
questionBank.exp: Capital provides infrastructure, supports business, and cushions losses (p.29).

questionBank.q: Bank capital serves as a buffer between:
opts: Shareholders and management.
Operating losses and depositors' funds.
Assets and liabilities.
Regulatory capital and economic capital.
questionBank.exp: Capital cushions the bank against operating losses, protecting depositors (p.29).

questionBank.q: The 'A' in CAMELS stands for:
opts: Asset Management.
Asset Quality.
Administrative.
Accounting.
questionBank.exp: A stands for Asset Quality (p.29).

questionBank.q: Asset quality refers to the productive capacity of assets, which includes:
opts: Intangible value and goodwill.
Income generation capacity and liquidity.
Market value and historical cost.
Collateral and security.
questionBank.exp: Productivity includes income generation and liquidity (p.29).

questionBank.q: Assets on a balance sheet are arranged in order of:
opts: Order of the risk attached to each category of asset.
Liquidity.
Order of how recently each asset was acquired.
Order of the monetary size of each asset.
questionBank.exp: Assets are arranged in order of liquidity (p.29).

questionBank.q: Liabilities are real and cannot be wished away, whereas assets:
opts: Recorded at historical cost, with revaluation prohibited by regulation.
May be unreal, stolen, or unrealisable.
Expected to generate income regardless of their productivity.
Arranged on the balance sheet by age of acquisition rather than liquidity.
questionBank.exp: Assets may be unreal, stolen, or unrealisable; they can be paper assets (p.29).

questionBank.q: Assets generate the most income for banks, but they also generate the largest losses depending on:
opts: The geographic location where the asset is held.
Their productivity.
The age of the asset since it was first acquired.
The monetary size of the individual asset.
questionBank.exp: Productivity determines income or loss (p.29).

questionBank.q: The 'M' in CAMELS stands for:
opts: Monetary Policy.
Management.
Margin.
Market Risk.
questionBank.exp: M stands for Management (p.30).

questionBank.q: Management is judged by the results of:
opts: Sensitivity to market risk.
All the other CAMELS parameters.
The bank's asset quality classification.
The bank's compliance with the single obligor limit.
questionBank.exp: Management is judged by results of the other parameters (p.30).

questionBank.q: Management drives:
opts: The calculation of foreign exchange risk exposure.
Financial intermediation and Asset and Liability Management.
The calculation of the capital adequacy ratio.
The preparation of statutory returns to the CBN.
questionBank.exp: Management drives financial intermediation and ALM (p.30).

questionBank.q: The 'E' in CAMELS stands for:
opts: Efficiency.
Earnings.
Equity.
Expense.
questionBank.exp: E stands for Earnings (p.30).

questionBank.q: Assets generate incomes for banks, while liabilities generate:
opts: Capital.
Costs.
Income.
Reserves.
questionBank.exp: Liabilities generate costs (p.30).

questionBank.q: Good earnings lead to:
opts: Higher operating costs for the bank.
Retained earnings, capital reserves, and dividends.
A reduction in the bank's liquidity position.
A reduction in the bank's overall capital.
questionBank.exp: Earnings generate retained earnings, reserves, and dividends (p.30).

questionBank.q: The 'L' in CAMELS stands for:
opts: Leverage.
Liquidity.
Loan.
Loss.
questionBank.exp: L stands for Liquidity (p.30).

questionBank.q: Liquidity refers to the ability of a bank to:
opts: Increase the volume of loans it extends to customers.
Meet maturing obligations without forced sale of assets at a loss.
Pay unusually high dividends to its shareholders.
Reduce the level of capital it holds.
questionBank.exp: Liquidity is ability to meet obligations without forced sale at loss (p.30).

questionBank.q: Liquidity also includes the ability to:
opts: Reduce the level of deposits it holds with the CBN.
Fund new assets or take advantage of investment opportunities.
Increase the cost at which it borrows funds in the interbank market.
Lower the level of capital it maintains.
questionBank.exp: Liquidity allows funding new assets and opportunities (p.30).

questionBank.q: The 'S' in CAMELS stands for:
opts: Stability.
Sensitivity to Market Risk.
Solvency.
Strategy.
questionBank.exp: S stands for Sensitivity to Market Risk (p.30).

questionBank.q: Market risks include:
opts: The risk of borrower default captured under loan loss provisioning.
Interest rate risk, exchange rate risk, and commodity price risk.
The risk of internal process failure addressed under corporate governance.
The risk of non-compliance with BOFIA addressed under sanctions.
questionBank.exp: Market risks include interest rate, exchange rate, and stock/commodity prices (p.30).

questionBank.q: Sensitivity to market risk examines:
opts: How much capital the bank holds relative to its assets.
How rate sensitive the bank's assets and liabilities are.
How profitable the bank has been over the period.
How liquid the bank's balance sheet currently is.
questionBank.exp: It looks at rate sensitivity of assets and liabilities and impact on income (p.30).

questionBank.q: The general role of bank supervisors includes:
opts: Deposit insurance and resolution-fund administration handled by the NDIC.
Preventive, curative, and liquidation roles.
Monetary policy formulation and currency issuance.
Advisory and legislative roles delegated to the Federal Ministry of Finance.
questionBank.exp: The three roles are preventive, curative, and liquidation (p.30-32).

questionBank.q: The preventive role includes ensuring that individuals with questionable integrity are precluded from banking through:
opts: Wealth.
Fit and proper person test.
Political affiliation.
Educational qualifications.
questionBank.exp: Fit and proper test is used (p.31).

questionBank.q: The preventive role also includes prescription of capital, which is important because:
opts: Capital adequacy is assessed once every three years alongside credit policy review.
Higher capital reduces the likelihood of failure.
Capital is irrelevant.
Lower capital increases profits.
questionBank.exp: Higher capital makes bank less likely to fail (p.31).

questionBank.q: Continuous supervision as a preventive measure includes:
opts: Special examinations triggered by depositor petitions.
On-site and off-site supervision.
Foreign exchange examinations checking compliance with forex rules.
Special investigations arising from suspected malpractice.
questionBank.exp: Continuous supervision involves both (p.31).

questionBank.q: Information disclosure is a preventive tool that requires banks to:
opts: Not disclose any information.
Announce operating results to the public.
Keep all information confidential.
Submit statutory returns to the Federal Ministry of Finance instead of the CBN.
questionBank.exp: Disclosure informs stakeholders (p.31).

questionBank.q: Imposition of sanctions is a preventive measure. Which of the following is a possible sanction?
opts: Payment of monetary penalty.
All of the above.
Removal of directors.
Suspension from clearing house.
questionBank.exp: Sanctions include fines, removal, suspension, takeover, revocation (p.31).

questionBank.q: The curative role aims to:
opts: Increasing the minimum capital requirements imposed on banks.
Correct anomalies and prevent loss of confidence.
Reducing the total number of banks operating in the system.
Issuing new banking licences to fresh entrants.
questionBank.exp: Curative role corrects anomalies (p.32).

questionBank.q: In the curative role, CBN may inject funds and take over management of troubled banks. This is an example of:
opts: Prevention.
Intervention.
Liquidation.
Licensing.
questionBank.exp: Intervention includes fund injection and management takeover (p.32).

questionBank.q: AMCON was set up to purchase toxic assets of ailing banks as part of:
opts: Regulatory role.
Curative role.
Preventive role.
Liquidation role.
questionBank.exp: AMCON is a curative measure (p.32).

questionBank.q: The liquidation role ensures:
opts: Closing the bank immediately without realising its assets.
Smooth and orderly winding up and best possible revenue for depositors.
Having the government take over all of the bank's assets.
Fully compensating the bank's shareholders for their losses.
questionBank.exp: Liquidation aims for orderly winding up and depositor protection (p.32).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of CAMELS?
opts: Sensitivity to Market Risk.
Efficiency.
Capital Adequacy.
Asset Quality.
questionBank.exp: CAMELS includes Capital, Asset quality, Management, Earnings, Liquidity, Sensitivity to market risk. Efficiency is not a component (p.29-30).

questionBank.q: The 'M' in CAMELS is judged by the results of the other parameters, implying that:
opts: Management is judged independently of the bank's other CAMELS parameters.
Management's performance is reflected in capital, asset quality, earnings, liquidity, and sensitivity.
Management is not important.
Management quality is assessed independently of the bank's asset quality alone.
questionBank.exp: Management is judged by the results of all other parameters (p.30).

questionBank.q: Earnings from assets generate profits that lead to:
opts: Higher operating costs for the bank.
Retained earnings and increased capital.
A decline in the quality of the bank's assets.
A reduction in the bank's liquidity position.
questionBank.exp: Profits lead to retained earnings, reserves, and dividends (p.30).

questionBank.q: Liquidity is important because it ensures a bank can:
opts: Increase lending without regard to available funding.
Meet maturing obligations without distress.
Reduce the level of capital it holds.
Pay unusually high dividends to its shareholders.
questionBank.exp: Liquidity is the ability to meet obligations without forced sale at loss (p.30).

questionBank.q: Sensitivity to market risk assesses the impact of changes in:
opts: The classification of loans as performing or non-performing.
Interest rates, exchange rates, and commodity prices.
The productivity and liquidity of the bank's asset base.
The bank's compliance with the single obligor limit.
questionBank.exp: Market risks include all three (p.30).

questionBank.q: The preventive role includes entry point screening to:
opts: Increasing the total number of banks in the system.
Prevent undesirable persons from owning or managing banks.
Encouraging greater foreign investment in banks.
Reducing the minimum capital requirements for new banks.
questionBank.exp: Entry point screening prevents undesirable persons (p.31).

questionBank.q: The failure of banks in the recent past is indicative of:
opts: A period of unusually high profitability across the sector.
Failure of the preventive strategy.
A period marked by excessive regulatory oversight.
The overall success of the preventive regulatory strategy.
questionBank.exp: Failure indicates failure of preventive strategy (p.31).

questionBank.q: Risk-based capital aims to encourage banks to keep:
opts: Low levels of capital relative to risk-weighted assets.
Sufficient cushion of equity capital and reserves.
High levels of debt relative to shareholders' funds.
Minimal reserves set aside against potential losses.
questionBank.exp: Risk-based capital encourages sufficient capital cushion (p.31).

questionBank.q: Disclosure of operating results to the public ensures:
opts: Reduced regulation.
Informed stakeholders.
Lower costs.
Increased profits.
questionBank.exp: Disclosure informs governments, supervisors, depositors, investors (p.31).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a sanction that can be imposed on a bank?
opts: A reduction in the interest rates a bank may charge.
Suspension from foreign exchange transactions.
A reduction in the deposit insurance coverage available.
An increase in the bank's minimum capital requirement.
questionBank.exp: Suspension from forex transactions is a sanction (p.31).

questionBank.q: The curative role prevents:
opts: A reduction in the bank's regulatory capital.
Loss of confidence or run on banks.
An increase in the bank's reported profits.
The entry of new banks into the market.
questionBank.exp: Curative role prevents loss of confidence (p.32).

questionBank.q: The Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria (AMCON) was established to:
opts: Regulate stock exchanges and other capital market operators.
Purchase toxic risk assets of ailing banks.
Formulate and implement the CBN's monetary policy.
Provide deposit insurance to customers of licensed banks.
questionBank.exp: AMCON purchases toxic assets (p.32).

questionBank.q: The liquidation role is performed when:
opts: A bank opens a new branch.
A bank's licence is revoked.
A bank is profitable.
A bank declares dividends.
questionBank.exp: Liquidation is for failed banks with revoked licences (p.32).

questionBank.q: Effective collaboration by regulatory authorities is essential for:
opts: A general reduction in regulatory oversight.
Good corporate governance and safe banking.
Increased profitability for individual banks.
Lower capital requirements imposed on banks.
questionBank.exp: Collaboration ensures good governance and safety (p.32).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a risk heightened by non-compliance with laws?
opts: Reputational risk.
All of the above.
Credit risk.
Liquidity risk.
questionBank.exp: Non-compliance heightens credit, liquidity, operational, reputational, market, and legal risks (p.32).

questionBank.q: Banks and bankers are required to apply due care and skill and imbibe tenets of:
opts: Cost minimisation.
Sound corporate governance.
Profit maximisation.
Market dominance.
questionBank.exp: They must imbibe tenets of sound corporate governance (p.32).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a component of bank examination?
opts: Marketing strategies.
Evaluating risk management.
Staff performance reviews.
Customer satisfaction surveys.
questionBank.exp: Examination evaluates risk management (p.27).

questionBank.q: The CBN's adoption of Basel Accords is intended to align Nigeria with:
opts: Domestic laws.
International best practice.
Political objectives.
Regional standards.
questionBank.exp: Adoption aligns with international best practice (p.4).

questionBank.q: The CBN's foreign exchange management circulars are designed to check:
opts: The overall profitability of individual banks.
Capital flight and money laundering.
The interest rates banks charge on loans.
Loan growth.
questionBank.exp: They check capital flight and money laundering (p.23-24).

questionBank.q: The Prudential Guidelines require that a bank's board of directors approve the credit policy and review it at least every three years. This ensures:
opts: An increase in the bank's market share.
Up-to-date risk management.
A reduction in the bank's operating costs.
Higher profits for the bank's shareholders.
questionBank.exp: Regular review ensures up-to-date risk management (p.19).

questionBank.q: A bank that fails to obtain CBN approval for opening a branch may face:
opts: No consequences.
Penalties under BOFIA.
Increased capital requirements.
A downward revision of the bank's risk rating under CAMELS.
questionBank.exp: Section 6 requires prior consent; violations attract penalties (p.13).

questionBank.q: The Banking Sector Resolution Fund is used to provide credit facilities to banks under resolution. This is part of:
opts: Licensing role.
Curative role.
Preventive role.
Liquidation role.
questionBank.exp: Resolution Fund supports resolution measures, which is curative (p.18).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a type of market risk?
opts: Legal risk.
Exchange rate risk.
Operational risk.
Credit risk.
questionBank.exp: Market risks include exchange rate, interest rate, and commodity price risk (p.30).

questionBank.q: The 'S' in CAMELS is often referred to as:
opts: Strategy.
Sensitivity to Market Risk.
Stability.
Solvency.
questionBank.exp: S stands for Sensitivity to Market Risk (p.30).

questionBank.q: The preventive role of bank supervisors includes:
opts: Purchase of toxic assets.
Prescription of capital.
Injecting funds into banks.
Liquidation of banks.
questionBank.exp: Preventive includes capital prescription, licensing, supervision, disclosure, sanctions (p.31).

questionBank.q: The curative role includes:
opts: Issuing new licences.
Taking over management.
Prescribing capital.
Conducting fit and proper tests.
questionBank.exp: Curative includes taking over management and injecting funds (p.32).

questionBank.q: The liquidation role is concerned with:
opts: Preventing bank failures before they occur.
Winding up failed banks and realising assets.
Ensuring the ongoing profitability of the affected bank.
Increasing the capital held by the affected bank.
questionBank.exp: Liquidation deals with winding up failed banks (p.32).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a consequence of non-compliance with banking regulations?
opts: A reduction in the penalties for non-compliance.
Removal and blacklisting of officers.
Increased public trust in the offending institution.
Higher capital adequacy for the offending institution.
questionBank.exp: Non-compliance may lead to removal and blacklisting (p.32).

questionBank.q: The CBN's power to revoke a banking licence is a:
opts: A power that follows, rather than precedes, a bank going into liquidation.
Preventive and curative measure.
A power that requires prior approval of the Federal High Court.
A power exercised by the NDIC as liquidator, not the CBN.
questionBank.exp: Revocation can be preventive (deterrence) and curative (removing failing banks) (p.31-32).

questionBank.q: The 'fit and proper person' test is used to:
opts: Determining the interest rate terms of a loan.
Evaluate the integrity of shareholders and managers.
Assessing the profitability of the bank's operations.
Setting the interest rates a bank may charge.
questionBank.exp: It prevents undesirable persons from owning or managing banks (p.31).

questionBank.q: Capital adequacy as a preventive measure is measured by:
opts: The ratio of loans to deposits.
The ratio of capital to risk-weighted assets.
The ratio of income to expenses.
The ratio of assets to liabilities.
questionBank.exp: Capital adequacy is capital relative to risk-weighted assets (p.31).

questionBank.q: The CBN's injection of funds into troubled banks is an example of:
opts: Liquidation role.
Curative role.
Supervisory role.
Preventive role.
questionBank.exp: Injection of funds is curative (p.32).

questionBank.q: AMCON was established to purchase toxic assets. This is part of:
opts: Licensing role.
Curative role.
Liquidation role.
Preventive role.
questionBank.exp: AMCON is a curative measure (p.32).

questionBank.q: The liquidation role aims to protect:
opts: Management.
Depositors.
Employees.
Shareholders.
questionBank.exp: Liquidation aims to protect depositors from avoidable loss (p.32).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a component of market risk?
opts: Operational risk.
Interest rate risk.
Credit risk.
Reputational risk.
questionBank.exp: Interest rate risk is a market risk (p.30).

questionBank.q: The CAMELS parameter 'Liquidity' is assessed by:
opts: The level of capital the bank holds relative to its risk-weighted assets.
Ability to meet obligations without forced asset sale.
The bank's earnings performance over the reporting period.
The quality of the loans held on the bank's balance sheet.
questionBank.exp: Liquidity is ability to meet obligations without distress (p.30).

questionBank.q: The 'A' in CAMELS, Asset Quality, is determined by:
opts: The number of employees.
The productive capacity of assets.
The size of the bank.
The location of branches.
questionBank.exp: Asset quality is about productive capacity (p.29).

questionBank.q: The CBN's use of CAMELS parameters is consistent with:
opts: Political objectives.
International best practice in bank supervision.
Domestic accounting standards.
Marketing strategies.
questionBank.exp: CAMELS is an internationally recognised supervisory framework (p.29).

questionBank.q: The Basel Committee's 29 Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision are organised around four distinct arrangements. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
opts: Legal and institutional structure for implementing public policy in the financial sector.
A monetary policy structure for setting interest rates and money supply targets.
A safety net arrangement for handling liquidity and solvency difficulties.
A supervisory structure to ensure that rules and regulations are adhered to.
questionBank.exp: The four arrangements are legal/institutional structure, regulatory structure, supervisory structure, and safety net arrangement. Monetary policy structure is not one of them (Trainee Manual, p.10).

questionBank.q: Banking regulation generally focuses on four key areas. Which of the following correctly lists them?
opts: Monetary policy, fiscal policy, exchange rate policy, and trade policy.
Licensing and supervision, market discipline, prudential requirements, and failure resolution processes.
Shareholder relations, marketing strategy, staff welfare, and branch expansion.
Interest rate setting, currency issuance, foreign reserves, and government advisory services.
questionBank.exp: The general principles of regulation cover licensing and supervision, market discipline, prudential requirements, and failure resolution processes (Trainee Manual, p.12).

questionBank.q: Under the Capital Adequacy component of CAMELS, what is a key function of bank capital?
opts: It determines the interest rate the bank charges on all its loans.
It cushions the bank against operating losses, buffering depositors' funds.
It replaces the need for the bank to hold any liquid assets.
It is recorded as a liability of the bank owed back to its owners.
questionBank.exp: Bank capital provides infrastructure and fixed assets, supports the volume and character of business, and cushions the bank against operating losses, buffering depositors' funds (Trainee Manual, p.29).
